title: Managing a doe on kindling day
subtitle: Checking the nest box and supporting a doe through birth.
excerpt: Kindling is the term for a rabbit doe giving birth. The process is usually quick and unassisted, taking 15 to 30 minutes from first kit to last. Your job is to have the nest box ready beforehand, give the doe privacy during birth, and carry out a brief check of the litter within the first few hours.
sourceNotes: Bob Bennett, Storey's Guide to Raising Rabbits (5th edn., 2009), kindling chapter. British Rabbit Council, Rabbit Husbandry Standards (2022). RSPCA, Breeding Rabbits: Guidance for Farmers (2019).

glossaryTerms.definition: The process of a rabbit doe giving birth to a litter of kits.
A newborn or young rabbit, especially in the context of a litter.
A partially enclosed box placed in the doe's cage before kindling, where she builds her nest from hay and her own pulled fur.

content.text: A doe that has been bred will give birth between day 28 and day 33 of gestation, most often on day 31. She needs a nest box, privacy, and clean dry bedding. Most does
in the early morning before the hutch is disturbed. Prepare for the expected date and check the nest box shortly after.

in the doe's cage on day 26 or 27 of gestation. Fill it two-thirds deep with clean meadow hay. The doe will then pull fur from her belly and dewlap in the 24 to 48 hours before kindling, adding it on top of the hay to create a warm insulated cup for the litter.
The nest box should be large enough for the doe to enter and turn around, but not so large that
scatter into the corners. A wooden box 40 cm x 25 cm x 25 cm with an entry cut partway up one end is the standard design for medium breeds.

Leave the doe alone. Disturbance during kindling is the most common cause of a doe cannibalising or abandoning her litter. Check the nestbox from a distance. If kindling takes more than 60 minutes from first signs to last kit, call your vet. Dystocia (a stuck kit) is rare in rabbits but can be fatal.
Wait at least 2 hours after the doe settles before opening the nest box. Rub your hands on the nest hay first so the kits smell familiar.
Remove any dead kits. They will chill quickly and, if left, can cause infection in the nest.
Check that the live kits are warm and plump. A cold kit can often be revived by warming it in your hands for 5 to 10 minutes, then replacing it in the centre of the nest under the fur blanket.
Count the litter and record it. Average litter size for most breeds is 4 to 10 kits. A doe has 8 to 10 functioning teats; litters larger than this need careful management.

Does nurse once per day, typically in the early morning. Kits that are feeding have round, tight bellies. Kits that have not fed have wrinkled skin on the neck and back. If kits have not fed by day 2, check whether the doe has milk by gently pressing the teat; a doe with mastitis or no milk needs veterinary attention.

attrs.cue: Kits are scattered around the cage outside the nest box
attrs.cause: Doe was disturbed during kindling and abandoned the nest, or the nest box entry is too high
attrs.fix: Return kits to the nest box and cover them with the fur layer. Reduce disturbance. Ensure the nest box entry cut is low enough for kits to re-enter if they crawl out.

attrs.cue: Doe has built no nest and pulled no fur by day 28
attrs.cause: False pregnancy, or the doe was not successfully bred
attrs.fix: A false pregnancy resolves on its own; no litter will arrive. Confirm whether the doe was actually mated. If she was mated and is on day 33 with no kits, she has likely reabsorbed the litter.
